Herman’s little toy was not getting in his way today. He reached for Uroboros, to bolster his speed and clear the area faster. The sooner he found the survivors, the sooner he could take them down and get back to the station. He felt the lift of energy, and without warning, the burning returned at the back of his neck, and the power was simply gone. The virus stilled. No writhing beneath the veins, no familiar burn gathering in his muscles. His healing edge dulled and vanished. His body felt heavier, slower. For the first time in years, he felt only human. He froze mid-stride, disbelief flashing sharp enough to cut. He tried again, reaching inward, demanding Uroboros answer. Nothing. Only the faint, mocking hum of the cuff at his wrist. The survivors noticed quickly. Ace darted across his vision, vaulting clean over a pallet. Wesker followed — slower, clumsier. When he reached for Uroboros to close the gap, his body refused. Wesker’s swing landed late, his knife bouncing off the wood, and Ace slipped free, laughing as he went. Nearby, Jake hesitated before bolting off a generator, his eyes flicking back in confusion. Uncertainty etched across his face, as if he had just seen a god limping across the cornfield; but even he eventually joined in on the easy run. Meg launched herself into the nearby shack and out of reach of his knife. He tried vaulting after her, legs refusing to align right mid-air, catching hard on the frame. Pain bloomed in his ribs as he hit the ground awkwardly. A window he once cleared with ease — now an obstacle. The Entity’s presence pressed heavy in his skull, cold and merciless, the spot on his neck flaring with heat. He reached back and felt at it, tracing the raised edges of a shape like a brand that had appeared out of nowhere. A set of jagged marks in small circle with a line. The Entity’s power limiter. He understood at once. This was punishment. Results had fallen. Quota unmet. She didn’t need to speak. Her judgment seeped from the soil, burned in the light, echoed in every missed strike. She was the Fog. The trial. The world. And she had deemed him insufficient. Earn them back, the whisper seemed to curl through the Fog. Prove your worth. Wesker’s teeth ground hard enough to ache. To be sabotaged by Herman was intolerable. But to be stripped bare by the Entity herself — reduced, grounded like a wayward child — was a degradation beyond measure. He forced himself onward, each step a weight. His fists still struck with brutal strength, but it was not the same. Every hook was slower. Every chase longer. The laughter of survivors rang sharper, crueler. They weren’t just surviving. They were enjoying it. And somewhere, Herman watched the data roll in, scribbling notes with delight as the great predator was left to flail as nothing more than flesh and bone. It didn’t take long for the difference to cut deep. Wesker still moved faster than any human had the right to. He still hit harder, his body honed by years of merciless conditioning. But without Uroboros threading his veins, his rhythm faltered. Every vault was mistimed, every chase a second too long. His instincts screamed to strike, to surge forward with inhuman speed — but his limbs betrayed him, sluggish and dull. Every second dragged with the weight of a body that no longer obeyed. The survivors capitalized on the situation. Pallets slammed into his shoulders, blast mines seared his vision, vaults taunted him just out of reach. He should have been untouchable, a storm breaking across the map. Instead, he felt like a blunt instrument swung too late. The cuff was infinitely worse now. Built for a monster, it tore straight through a man. Each shock locked his muscles longer; each jolt scrambled his vision harder. Chemical injections lingered in his system, refusing to flush out. His breath hitched in sharp coughs, his chest spasmed in arrhythmic bursts, sweat stinging his eyes as the toxins dragged him down. By mid-trial he was bleeding from pallet splinters and generator traps, staggering where once he would have walked unmarked. Hooks came harder, slower. The laughter of survivors at the exit gate carried like knives. He clenched his fists, refusing to yield, even as his knees trembled beneath him. Pride alone kept him moving, a stubborn refusal to collapse. But each pulse of the cuff reminded him — without Uroboros, without his healing, without his edge — he would just bleed out like any other man. And Herman’s notes would be exquisite. The Fog reclaimed its pieces when the trial ended. Survivors were carried back to the fire, laughing and shaken, while Wesker retreated into the station’s darkened corners. Normally the cycle reset him whole. Bruises gone, cuts erased, breath restored. Not this time. The cuff’s bite carried over. His chest still spasmed with every uneven beat, lungs dragging against phantom smoke from trapped generators. His vision twitched in static bursts, a faint afterimage of the Fog’s glare lingering at the corners of his eyes. The chemicals burned in his veins, heavier now that his body couldn’t purge them quickly. He fought the instinct to retch against it. It wouldn’t help, that much he could tell. For the first time in years, Wesker stayed broken between trials. Overhead, Herman’s voice slid through the intercom, muffled by the scratch of a pen. “Subject 06-W, post-trial observation. Damage persisting beyond reset cycle. Viral regression absolute. Healing factor absent. Collateral injuries amplified.” A pause, and the click of a smile audible behind the speaker. “Entity tolerance noted. No intervention to preserve asset.
